request: why do two parallel vectors only span a line and not the whole plane

beats.intent: Two arrows v = (2, 1) and w = (-3, -1.5) lying along one line
beats.narration: Take v, two across and one up, and w, which points the opposite way along the very same line.
beats.code:
stage.title("Span of parallel vectors")
p = draw_plane(stage)
v = draw_vector(stage, p, (2, 1))
w = draw_vector(stage, p, (-3, -1.5), color=ORANGE)
stage.caption("Yellow v, orange w = -1.5 v")

beats.intent: v stretched and flipped, its tip sliding along the same line
beats.narration: Scale v by any number: it grows, shrinks or flips, but its tip never leaves that line.
beats.code:
scale_vector(stage, p, v, 1.5)
scale_vector(stage, p, v, -0.5)
stage.caption("Every multiple of v stays on its line")

beats.intent: The span drawn as one blue line through the origin
beats.narration: Every combination a v plus b w lands on this one line: that line is the whole span.
beats.code:
ln = draw_span(stage, p, (2, 1))
pulse(stage, ln)
stage.caption("All combinations av + bw lie on this line")

beats.intent: A red vector u = (-1, 2) off the line that no combination reaches
beats.narration: A vector off the line, like u, can never be built from v and w, because w adds no new direction.
beats.code:
u = draw_vector(stage, p, (-1, 2), color=RED, label="u")
stage.equation(r"a\vec{v} + b\vec{w} = (a - 1.5b)\,\vec{v}", where="right")

request: what does changing to a new basis look like in 2D

beats.intent: The standard grid with i-hat, j-hat and the vector v = (3, 1)
beats.narration: In the usual basis, v is three steps along i-hat and one step along j-hat.
beats.code:

p = draw_plane(stage)
i_hat, j_hat = draw_basis(stage, p)
v = draw_vector(stage, p, (3, 1))
stage.caption("Standard coordinates: v = (3, 1)")

beats.intent: A teal grid spanned by b1 = (1, 1) and b2 = (-1, 1) laid over the plane
beats.narration: Now pick two new basis vectors, b1 and b2. Their multiples draw a tilted grid of their own.
beats.code:
stage.clear(keep=[p, v])
grid, b1, b2 = basis_grid(stage, p, (1, 1), (-1, 1))
stage.caption("New basis: b1 = (1, 1), b2 = (-1, 1)")

beats.intent: v reached by two steps along b1 and one step back along b2
beats.narration: To reach v on the new grid, go two steps along b1, then one step backwards along b2.
beats.code:
s1 = draw_vector(stage, p, (2, 2), color=GREEN)
s2 = draw_arrow(stage, p.c2p(2, 2), p.c2p(3, 1), color=RED)
stage.caption("v = 2 b1 - 1 b2")

beats.intent: The same arrow v with new coordinates (2, -1), as a matrix product
beats.narration: So the same arrow has new coordinates two and minus one. The matrix with b1 and b2 as columns turns them back into three and one.
beats.code:
stage.clear(keep=[p, v, s1, s2])
stage.equation(r"\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\ -1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3\\ 1\end{bmatrix}", where="right")

request: what are the eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix

f = lambda x: 0.5 * x + 1
g = plot_graph(stage, ax, f, label="y = 0.5x + 1")

beats.intent: A tangent sliding along the line, its slope reading 0.50 the whole way

run1 = draw_line(stage, ax.c2p(0, 1), ax.c2p(2, 1), color=GREEN)
rise1 = draw_line(stage, ax.c2p(2, 1), ax.c2p(2, 2), color=RED)
run2 = draw_line(stage, ax.c2p(3, 2.5), ax.c2p(5, 2.5), color=GREEN)
rise2 = draw_line(stage, ax.c2p(5, 2.5), ax.c2p(5, 3.5), color=RED)

stage.label(rise1, "1", direction=RIGHT, color=RED)
stage.label(run2, "2", direction=DOWN, color=GREEN)

beats.intent: Rise over run written out: one over two
beats.narration: Rise over run is one over two wherever you measure it, so the slope is constant.
beats.code: stage.equation(r"m = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{1}{2}", where="right")

request: find the gcd of 21 and 15 by subtracting the smaller from the larger

stage.play(FadeOut(bars[2]))
for a, b in [(6, 15), (6, 9), (6, 3), (3, 3)]:
    stage.play(bars[0].animate.stretch_to_fit_height(a / 21 * 4, about_edge=DOWN), bars[1].animate.stretch_to_fit_height(b / 21 * 4, about_edge=DOWN), run_time=0.8)

stage.clear()
u = 0.24
R = Rectangle(width=21 * u, height=15 * u, color=WHITE).move_to([-3.2, -0.1, 0])
stage.play(Create(R))
corner = R.get_corner(DL)
tiles = [(0, 0, 15, BLUE), (15, 0, 6, GREEN), (15, 6, 6, GREEN), (15, 12, 3, YELLOW), (18, 12, 3, YELLOW)]
squares = [Square(side_length=s * u, color=col, fill_opacity=0.5).move_to(corner + np.array([(x + s / 2) * u, (y + s / 2) * u, 0])) for x, y, s, col in tiles]
for sq in squares:
    stage.play(FadeIn(sq), run_time=0.6)
stage.caption("Smallest square: 3 by 3")

beats.intent: The chain of gcds ending at 3
beats.narration: Subtracting never changes the greatest common divisor, so the gcd of 21 and 15 is 3.

stage.equation(r"\gcd(21, 15) = \gcd(6, 15)", r"= \gcd(6, 9) = \gcd(6, 3)", r"= \gcd(3, 3) = 3", where="right")
highlight(stage, squares[-1])

request: how does a parity bit detect a single bit error

highlight(stage, cells[15])
stage.caption("The last bit makes the count of 1s even")

beats.intent: Every 1 outlined: ten of them, an even count
beats.narration: The receiver counts the ones. Ten: even, so nothing looks wrong.

eq = stage.equation(r"\text{ones} = 10\ (\text{even})", where="right")

beats.intent: One bit flipped by noise, turned red: the count is now odd

stage.play(FadeOut(eq))
eq = stage.equation(r"\text{ones} = 9\ (\text{odd!})", where="right")
stage.caption("Odd count: an error is caught")

beats.intent: A second flip makes the count even again, and the error slips by
beats.narration: But flip a second bit and the count is even again. One parity bit catches any single flip, not two.
beats.code:

stage.play(Transform(cells[9][0], MathTex("0", font_size=36).move_to(cells[9])))
stage.play(FadeOut(eq))
eq = stage.equation(r"\text{ones} = 8\ (\text{even})", where="right")
stage.caption("Two flips cancel: this one goes unseen")
